title: Three-phase surge scan: latency + cost brief (draft)
body:
Purpose:
Run a compact benchmark that mimics a realistic three-phase surge (ramp -> peak -> taper) to observe how our serving runtime and a few model variants trade off p50/p90/p99 latency and marginal cost-per-query. This is meant as an early collateral draft we can iterate into a slide or customer-facing note.

Topline findings (summary):
- Under the same reserved capacity, workloads that follow a fast ramp + sustained peak (phase 2) expose two primary cost leaks: 1) reduced batching efficiency during ramp, 2) tail amplification due to slot contention at p99.
- Quantized model variants (int8/hybrid-4) reduce per-token cost by ~18–28% on steady-state peak, but during ramp the effective savings drop to ~8–12% because of sequence-length variability and less KV cache reuse.
- Small session prewarm (warmup windows of ~30s for bursty sessions) recovers a lot of p99 pain while costing <3% additional steady-state spend if scheduled opportunistically.

Experiment design (short):
- Workload: synthetic session traces derived from production sampling (anon). Each trace contains up to 6 turns, token lengths drawn from empirical distribution (median 34 tokens, tail 400+ tokens).
- Surge pattern: three phases, 10m total:
  * Phase 1 (ramp, 2m): linear ramp from baseline 10 qps to peak 400 qps
  * Phase 2 (peak, 6m): sustained 400 qps with burst microspikes +/- 20% every 30s
  * Phase 3 (taper, 2m): linear drop back to 10 qps
- Models tested: rdl-7b (fp16), rdl-7b-int8, rdl-13b (fp16), rdl-13b-hybrid4
- Serving config knobs: batch size cap (1, 8, 32), session affinity on/off, prewarm window (0s/30s), kv-cache enabled/disabled
- Environment: Dedicated pool (8x A100 equivalent instances), same infra allocation across runs, instrumentation via tracewalk + slotization logs

Key numeric table (excerpt) — p50/p90/p99 latencies in ms and cost in $ per 1k queries (steady-state peak segment):

Model | batch cap=8 | p50 | p90 | p99 | $/1k q
------|-------------|-----|-----|-----|--------
rdl-7b (fp16)       |    8     |  48 | 112 | 240 | 1.02
rdl-7b-int8         |    8     |  52 | 125 | 300 | 0.82
rdl-13b (fp16)      |    8     |  95 | 210 | 460 | 1.94
rdl-13b-hybrid4     |    8     | 110 | 250 | 560 | 1.48

Notes on the table: cost numbers include GPU amortized cost + estimated memory overhead; they are directional (not billing-accurate). p99 inflation for quantized variants is larger than fp16 as our kernel selection currently prioritizes throughput.

Ramp vs steady-state snapshot (qualitative ascii charts):
- Batch efficiency (mean tokens per batch) across time (phase 1 -> 2 -> 3):
  Phase 1: |||     (low: 1.8 tokens/batch)
  Phase 2: ||||||||||||||   (high: 9.6 tokens/batch)
  Phase 3: |||     (back to 2.1 tokens/batch)

- p99  (relative bars):
  rdl-7b (fp16):  |||||||||||||||| (baseline 240ms)
  rdl-7b-int8:    |||||||||||||||||||| (300ms)
  rdl-13b (fp16): |||||||||||||||||||||||||| (460ms)
  rdl-13b-hyb4:   |||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||| (560ms)

Interpretation / hypotheses:
- Ramp inefficiency: when qps increases quickly the batching window is starved; requests are served at smaller effective batch sizes which increases per-query GPU cost. This effect is acute when the session mix has many short interactions (we observed p50 increases on ramp of ~15–25% relative to steady state).
- KV cache reuse: quantized variants have slightly different tokenization/kcache layout which reduced cache hit probability by ~4–6% in our run; caching losses explain some of the diminishing returns for int8 during the peak.
- Tail biler: slot contention and opportunistic slot stealing under high concurrency create stragglers — these are the main driver of p99 variance. Prewarm windows that pin a small number of slots to high-probability tenants can cut p99 by up to 30% for minimal cost.

Operational implications:
- For customer tiers that require p99 SLOs, recommend defaulting to a small prewarm budget and conservative quantization suggestions (hybrid4 preferred to plain int8 for long-conversation workloads).
- For best $/1k in heavy steady-state use, quantized variants are preferred but only after we (a) tune kernel selection for int8 p99, and (b) improve KV cache alignment.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Is the int8 kernel scheduling gap fixable via a different micro-batching strategy without sacrificing throughput? (Run A/B with modified scheduler)
- How does multi-tenant slotization mix alter these results? We tested on a reserved homogeneous pool; mixing with a noisy tenant could amplify tail.
- Can a predictive prewarm policy (based on short-term qps slope) recover ramp inefficiency without costing steady-state?

Proposed next steps (short roadmap):
1) Re-run the same three-phase pattern against mixed-tenant pool (INF-1305) — add tenancy noise. Owner: Miguel — target 2027-05-12.
2) Kernel-scheduler A/B with int8 micro-batching tweaks — owner: Ben — target 2027-05-20.
3) Prototype predictive prewarm (rule: slope>50 qps in 30s triggers N slots) and test cost delta — owner: Priya — target 2027-05-24.

Appendix (instrumentation snippets & raw observations):
- Observed mean batch size (rdl-7b-int8) during ramp: 2.3 -> during peak: 8.9 -> taper: 2.5
- KV cache hit: fp16 ~72%, int8 ~68% (sampled TTL 5m)
- Tail anomaly timestamps: list attached in linked artifact (github PR 2034 contains raw traces)

Notes to self / document TODOs:
- Turn this into a two-slide customer-facing piece (one slide topline + recommended knobs; one slide ascii charts + caveats).
- Add a small callout that $/1k here is internal modeling and doesn't include infra networking or storage ops billing.
- Cross-link to Dedicated SLA docs and the rollout playbook.

Unresolved / rough bits:
- Cost per 1k uses a simplified amort model — reconcile with finance for external comms.
- Should we promote hybrid4 as "recommended" for medium-length sessions? need approval from research team (Priya).

Contact: Laura Chen (product-optimize) — ping in #prod-optimize or DM for clarifications.

End of draft.
